# toolchain — the tools a check needs before it can be a check

Gate A is not "the code looks right". It is "the command ran, and it passed". A
command that is not installed cannot run, so the honest state of that work is
`blocked`.

This skill removes that excuse. It finds what is missing, proposes one command,
asks, installs, and then proves the result.

**Find out before the work, not after it.** A missing linter discovered at the
end of a task turns finished work into blocked work.

## Step 1 — Find out what is missing

```bash
bin/craft-toolchain
```

It changes nothing. It reads `config/toolchain.json`, checks `PATH`, and prints
one line per tool: `OK` with the path, or `MISSING` with the exact install
command for the installer it detected.

Exit code 1 means a **required** tool is missing. Required means
`config/workflow.md` §6 names it, and a check depends on it.

`bin/craft-doctor` reports the same gap from the other side, as a `FAIL` in its
`commands` group. Either one is a reason to load this skill.

## Step 2 — Decide where the tool belongs

Read the `note` line first. This is the question that is easy to get wrong.

When §6 runs a check inside a container, for example
`docker compose exec web pytest`, **installing on the host does not put the
tool in the container.** A host copy helps you while you work. It does not make
the checkpoint command run.

- The check runs **in the container** → the package belongs in the image or in
  the requirements file it builds from. Say so, and hand that change to the
  developer. Do not edit those files to make a check pass.
- The check runs **on the host** → continue to step 3.

Say which of the two this is before you propose anything.

## Step 3 — Show the plan, and ask

Never install without asking. Installing software changes the developer's
machine, and the right place for a package is a decision they own.

State four things in one short block:

1. Which tools are missing, and whether each one is required or optional.
2. The installer that was detected, and why that one.
3. The exact commands that will run.
4. Whether any of them changes a file this repository tracks.

That last point matters. `poetry add` and `pipenv install` write the dependency
into `pyproject.toml` or `Pipfile`, which is a change to the repository, not to
the machine. `bin/craft-toolchain` refuses those two until
`--allow-repo-change` is passed. Do not pass that flag on your own initiative.

Then stop and wait.

## Step 4 — Install

```bash
bin/craft-toolchain --install            # the required tools
bin/craft-toolchain --install --all      # the optional ones as well
bin/craft-toolchain --manager pipx       # override the detected installer
```

Each command is printed before it runs, and the first failure stops the rest.

When the developer's repository has its own way of installing development
dependencies, use that instead, and say that you did. A repository that pins its
tools has a reason.

## Step 5 — Prove it

```bash
bin/craft-toolchain
bin/craft-doctor
```

Both must agree that the tool is there. **Do not report the tooling as fixed
until a command you ran says so.** That is the same rule the rest of this
workflow follows, applied to the tooling.

Then run the check that was blocked, and report its real result.

## What this skill will not do

- It will not install `yapf`. `config/workflow.md` §6 says never `yapf`, and
  `standards/python_code_style.ai.md` picks `black` or `pyink`. Refuse this
  whoever asks, and name the standard.
- It will not install anything before the developer agrees.
- It will not add a dependency to `pyproject.toml`, `Pipfile`, `poetry.lock`,
  `requirements.txt` or a Dockerfile to make a check pass. It reports the change
  and lets the developer decide.
- It will not report a check as passing because the tool is now installed. The
  tool being present and the check passing are two different facts.
- It will not silently pick a different tool. If `pylint` cannot be installed, it
  says `pylint` is missing. It does not substitute `ruff` and carry on.

## When the install cannot happen

Some machines have no package index, no network, or an externally managed Python
that refuses `pip install`. `bin/craft-toolchain` names that last case
explicitly.

When the tool cannot be installed, the answer is not to work around it:

1. Say which tool, and why the install failed.
2. Say which check is therefore impossible.
3. Report the work as `blocked`, and name the command that did not run.

An unrunnable check is a known gap. A check reported as passed without running is
a false statement, and this workflow exists to stop that one.

## Adding a tool to the wanted set

Edit `config/toolchain.json`, not `bin/craft-toolchain`. Each entry names an
`id`, a `purpose`, its `source` in `config/workflow.md`, whether it is
`required`, and an `any_of` list of commands that satisfy it with the package
behind each one. A tool is satisfied when any one of its commands is on `PATH`,
which is how the Format row means "detect `black` or `pyink`".

`config/workflow.md` stays the human-readable source. Change the §6 row first,
then match it here.
